Allow
al-lou'
v. (in the Authorized Version: to approve, to sanction, to consent to as right — not merely to permit)
From Latin allaudare, to praise, crossed in English with allocare, to place or assign. The seventeenth-century sense that dominates the Authorized Version is the first: to allow a thing is to approve it, to give it your voice, which is why Romans 7:15 cannot be read with the modern meaning.

Biblical Definition

This is one of the words a modern reader will certainly misread unless he is warned. “For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I” (Rom 7:15). Paul is not saying that he does not permit his own actions, which would be nonsense; he is saying he does not approve them — the Greek is ginosko, to know or acknowledge, and the sense is that the regenerate man refuses to own the sin he still commits. That is the mark of the new nature: not sinlessness, but the settled disowning of the sin. Our Lord uses the word the same way against the scribes: “ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres” (Luk 11:48). Building a prophet's tomb while sharing his murderers' heart is not permission, it is endorsement, and it is the charge. Paul before Felix uses it of shared confession: the resurrection is a hope “which they themselves also allow” (Act 24:15) — the Pharisees granted it, owned it, held it with him. To allow, in this Book, is to say amen to a thing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines allow first as to grant, give or yield; and second as to approve, to justify, to sanction — citing Romans 7:15 for the sense of approbation.

expand to see more

ALLOW, v.t. To grant, give or yield; as, to allow a servant his liberty.

1. To admit; as, to allow the truth of a proposition.

2. To approve, justify or sanction. Ye allow the deeds of your fathers. Luke 11.

3. To afford; to grant; to permit; to suffer to be done.

ALLOWANCE, n. Approbation; sanction; license.

Key Scripture

Rom 7:15 — "For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I."

Luk 11:48 — "Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres."

Act 24:15 — "And have hope toward God, which they themselves also allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust."

Modern Corruption

Read with the modern sense of “permit,” Romans 7:15 becomes an excuse for sin instead of the mark of a new heart.

expand to see more

A reader who imports today's meaning into Romans 7:15 gets a Paul who cannot help himself and is therefore not responsible — the verse becomes a shrug. The seventeenth-century sense gives the opposite. Paul says he does not approve what he does; the sin is committed and simultaneously disowned, hated, refused a vote. That refusal is precisely what the unregenerate man cannot produce and what the indwelling Spirit does produce. Romans 7 is not a permission slip; it is the anatomy of a war in a man who has been made new and is not yet made perfect.

The Luke 11 use guards the other flank. The scribes did nothing to the prophets; they merely built the sepulchres and approved. Scripture treats approval as participation — who knowing the judgment of God… not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them (Rom 1:32). In an age whose chief public act is the giving and withholding of approval, that verse is unnervingly current: a man is answerable for what he applauds, and building the monument can be its own confession.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ginosko (G1097), to know, acknowledge, own; suneudokeo (G4909), to consent, to approve together with; dokimazo (G1381), to test and approve.

expand to see more

Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, to recognize, to acknowledge as one's own; Romans 7:15, rendered allow in the sense of own or approve.

Greek suneudokeo (G4909) — to think well of together, to consent to; Luke 11:48, of consenting to the fathers' deeds; Acts 8:1, Saul was consenting unto his death.

Greek prosdechomai (G4327) — to receive, to accept, to look for; Acts 24:15, of the hope the Pharisees also owned.

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove, to test, to approve after testing; Romans 12:2, 1 Thessalonians 2:4.

Greek euarestos (G2101) — well-pleasing, acceptable; the standard by which a thing may rightly be allowed.

Usage

"“That which I do I allow not” — approve not, and there is the new heart."

"“Ye allow the deeds of your fathers” — approval counted as participation."

"“Which they themselves also allow” — a hope owned in common."
